title.en: Explain why correlation does not imply causation

say.en: When the price of tomatoes shoots up, families buy fewer. When a family's income rises, it spends more. Economists want to know how strongly such pairs of variables move together. In this lesson: Define correlation.
Distinguish positive and negative correlation.
Explain why correlation does not imply causation.

body.en: *Correlation* studies how two variables move together. It tells us the direction of the relationship (positive or negative) and its intensity (how close it is). It is measured by the coefficient of correlation $r$, which lies between $-1$ and $+1$.
body.kn: ಎರಡು ಚರಾಂಶಗಳು ಒಟ್ಟಿಗೆ ಹೇಗೆ ಚಲಿಸುತ್ತವೆ ಎಂಬುದನ್ನು ಸಹಸಂಬಂಧ ಅಧ್ಯಯನ ಮಾಡುತ್ತದೆ: ಸಂಬಂಧದ ದಿಕ್ಕು ಮತ್ತು ತೀವ್ರತೆ. ಎರಡೂ ಒಂದೇ ದಿಕ್ಕಿನಲ್ಲಿ ಚಲಿಸಿದರೆ ಧನಾತ್ಮಕ, ವಿರುದ್ಧ ದಿಕ್ಕಿನಲ್ಲಿ ಚಲಿಸಿದರೆ ಋಣಾತ್ಮಕ. ಸಹಸಂಬಂಧ ಗುಣಾಂಕ r, −1 ಮತ್ತು +1 ರ ನಡುವೆ ಇರುತ್ತದೆ.

points.en: Positive: both move in the same direction (income and consumption)
Negative: they move in opposite directions (price and quantity demanded)
r = +1 perfect positive; r = −1 perfect negative; r = 0 no linear *correlation*

narration.en: Correlation studies how two variables move together: the direction of their relationship and how strong it is. If both rise together it is positive; if one rises when the other falls it is negative. The coefficient r lies between minus one and plus one.

r = plus 1 perfect positive; r equals minus 1 perfect negative; r equals 0 no linear correlation.

narration.en: The teacher sketches a rising line and a falling line, then a scale of r from minus one to plus one.

say.en: On the left, income and consumption: as income rises, consumption rises. This is positive correlation.
On the right, price and quantity demanded: as price rises, demand falls. This is negative correlation.
We measure both direction and strength with one number, r. It always lies between minus one and plus one.
Minus one is perfect negative, zero is no linear correlation and plus one is perfect positive.
And remember: correlation does not prove causation. A third variable may move both.

body.en: *Correlation* only measures covariation; it does not show that one variable causes the other. Two variables may be correlated by chance, or because a third variable affects both. For example, ice-cream sales and drowning deaths both rise in summer because of hot weather.
body.kn: ಸಹಸಂಬಂಧವು ಒಂದು ಚರಾಂಶ ಇನ್ನೊಂದಕ್ಕೆ ಕಾರಣ ಎಂದು ಸಾಬೀತು ಮಾಡುವುದಿಲ್ಲ. ಅದು ಆಕಸ್ಮಿಕವಾಗಿರಬಹುದು ಅಥವಾ ಮೂರನೇ ಚರಾಂಶ ಎರಡರ ಮೇಲೂ ಪ್ರಭಾವ ಬೀರುತ್ತಿರಬಹುದು.

points.en: *Correlation* may be due to pure chance
A third variable may influence both

problem.en: Classify the correlation: (a) price of petrol and quantity bought, (b) height and weight of students, (c) rainfall and crop output in a dry district, (d) shoe size and marks in Economics.

steps.en: (a) Price rises, quantity bought falls: opposite directions, negative.
(b) Taller students usually weigh more: same direction, positive.
(c) More rain usually means more output in a dry district: positive.
(d) No sensible link: no correlation (any r found is by chance).

narration.en: Let us work this out together. Classify the correlation: (a) price of petrol and quantity bought, (b) height and weight of students, (c) rainfall and crop output in a dry district, (d) shoe size and marks in Economics.

say.en: Let us work this out together. Classify the correlation: a price of petrol and quantity bought, b height and weight of students, c rainfall and crop output in a dry district, d shoe size and marks in Economics.
a Price rises, quantity bought falls: opposite directions, negative.
b Taller students usually weigh more: same direction, positive.
c More rain usually means more output in a dry district: positive.
d No sensible link: no correlation any r found is by chance.
So the answer is a negative, b positive, c positive, d no correlation.
